claim: In 2019, there were 229 million cases of malaria worldwide, resulting in more than 400,000 deaths.
source: In 2019, there were 229 million cases of malaria worldwide, resulting in more than 400,000 deaths (WHO, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to WHO, 2020.

claim: About half of the world's population lives in malaria infection-prone areas.
source: Currently, about half of the world's population lives in infection-prone areas, and more than 90% of the malaria deaths occur in Africa.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the manuscript.

claim: More than 90% of malaria deaths occur in Africa.
source: Currently, about half of the world's population lives in infection-prone areas, and more than 90% of the malaria deaths occur in Africa.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the manuscript.

claim: Children under five years of age and pregnant women suffer from severe malaria disease.
source: In particular, children under five years of age and pregnant women suffer from severe disease, but adults from areas of lower endemicity and non-immune travelers are also vulnerable to severe malaria.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the manuscript.

claim: Adults from areas of lower endemicity and non-immune travelers are vulnerable to severe malaria.
source: In particular, children under five years of age and pregnant women suffer from severe disease, but adults from areas of lower endemicity and non-immune travelers are also vulnerable to severe malaria.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the manuscript.

claim: Anemia and convulsions are more frequent in children with severe malaria.
source: Anemia and convulsions are more frequent in children, jaundice indicative of hepatic dysfunction and oliguric renal failure are the dominant manifestations in adults (Dondorp et al., 2008; World Health Organization, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dondorp et al., 2008 and World Health Organization, 2014.

claim: Jaundice indicative of hepatic dysfunction and oliguric renal failure are the dominant manifestations of severe malaria in adults.
source: Anemia and convulsions are more frequent in children, jaundice indicative of hepatic dysfunction and oliguric renal failure are the dominant manifestations in adults (Dondorp et al., 2008; World Health Organization, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dondorp et al., 2008 and World Health Organization, 2014.

claim: Mortality from severe malaria increases with age.
source: Moreover, the mortality increases with age (Dondorp et al., 2008) and was previously determined as a risk factor for severe malaria and fatal outcome in non-immune patients, but the causing factors are largely unknown (Schwartz et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dondorp et al., 2008.

claim: Age was previously determined as a risk factor for severe malaria and fatal outcome in non-immune patients.
source: Moreover, the mortality increases with age (Dondorp et al., 2008) and was previously determined as a risk factor for severe malaria and fatal outcome in non-immune patients, but the causing factors are largely unknown (Schwartz et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schwartz et al., 2001.

claim: The causing factors for age as a risk factor for severe malaria in non-immune patients are largely unknown.
source: Moreover, the mortality increases with age (Dondorp et al., 2008) and was previously determined as a risk factor for severe malaria and fatal outcome in non-immune patients, but the causing factors are largely unknown (Schwartz et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is stated as a knowledge gap in the manuscript.

claim: The virulence of Plasmodium falciparum is linked to infected erythrocytes binding to endothelial cell surface molecules expressed on blood vessel walls.
source: The virulence of Plasmodium falciparum (P. falciparum) is linked to the infected erythrocytes binding to endothelial cell surface molecules expressed on blood vessel walls.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the manuscript.

claim: Sequestration prevents the passage of infected erythrocytes through the spleen.
source: This phenomenon, known as sequestration, prevents the passage of infected erythrocytes through the spleen, which would otherwise remove the infected erythrocytes from the circulation and kill the parasite (Saul, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Saul, 1999.

claim: The spleen would otherwise remove infected erythrocytes from the circulation and kill the parasite.
source: This phenomenon, known as sequestration, prevents the passage of infected erythrocytes through the spleen, which would otherwise remove the infected erythrocytes from the circulation and kill the parasite (Saul, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Saul, 1999.

claim: P. falciparum parasites have acquired several multi-copy gene families coding for variant surface antigens, allowing immune escape through extensive sequence polymorphisms.
source: The membrane proteins mediating sequestration are exposed to the host's immune system, and through evolution, P. falciparum parasites have acquired several multi-copy gene families coding for variant surface antigens, allowing immune escape through extensive sequence polymorphisms.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the manuscript.

claim: Endothelial sequestration is mediated by the P. falciparum erythrocyte membrane protein 1 (PfEMP1) family.
source: Endothelial sequestration is mediated by the P. falciparum erythrocyte membrane protein 1 (PfEMP1) family, the members of which have different binding capacities for host vascular tissue receptors such as CD36, endothelial protein C receptor (EPCR), ICAM-1, PECAM1, receptor for complement component C1q (gC1qR), and chondroitin sulphate (CSA) (Magallón-Tejada et al., 2016; Turner et al., 2013; Rowe et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Magallón-Tejada et al., 2016; Turner et al., 2013; Rowe et al., 2009.

claim: PfEMP1 family members have different binding capacities for host vascular tissue receptors such as CD36, EPCR, ICAM-1, PECAM1, gC1qR, and CSA.
source: Endothelial sequestration is mediated by the P. falciparum erythrocyte membrane protein 1 (PfEMP1) family, the members of which have different binding capacities for host vascular tissue receptors such as CD36, endothelial protein C receptor (EPCR), ICAM-1, PECAM1, receptor for complement component C1q (gC1qR), and chondroitin sulphate (CSA) (Magallón-Tejada et al., 2016; Turner et al., 2013; Rowe et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Magallón-Tejada et al., 2016; Turner et al., 2013; Rowe et al., 2009.

claim: The long, variable, extracellular PfEMP1 region responsible for receptor binding contains a single N-terminal segment (NTS) and a variable number of different Duffy binding-like (DBL) and cysteine-rich inter-domain region domains (CIDR).
source: The long, variable, extracellular PfEMP1 region responsible for receptor binding contains a single N-terminal segment (NTS; main classes A, B, and pam) and a variable number of different Duffy binding-like (DBL; main classes DBLα-ζ and pam) and cysteine-rich inter-domain region domains (CIDR; main classes CIDRα-δ and pam) (Rask et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rask et al., 2010.

claim: PfEMP1 molecules have been grouped into four categories (A, B, C, and E) depending on the type of N-terminal domains, the 5' upstream sequence, the chromosomal localization, and the direction of transcription of their encoding var gene.
source: PfEMP1 molecules have been grouped into four categories (A, B, C, and E) depending on the type of N-terminal domains (the PfEMP1 'head structure') as well as the 5' upstream sequence, the chromosomal localization, and the direction of transcription of their encoding var gene (Rask et al., 2010; Kyes et al., 2007; Kraemer and Smith, 2003; Lavstsen et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rask et al., 2010; Kyes et al., 2007; Kraemer and Smith, 2003; Lavstsen et al., 2003.

claim: Each parasite possesses about 60 var genes with approximately the same distribution among the different groups.
source: Each parasite possesses about 60 var genes with approximately the same distribution among the different groups (Rask et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rask et al., 2010.

claim: About 20% of PfEMP1 variants belong to group A.
source: About 20% of PfEMP1 variants belong to group A and are typically longer proteins with a head structure containing DBLα1 and either an EPCR-binding CIDRα1 domain or a CIDRβ/γ/δ domain of unknown function.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the manuscript.

claim: Group A PfEMP1 are typically longer proteins with a head structure containing DBLα1 and either an EPCR-binding CIDRα1 domain or a CIDRβ/γ/δ domain of unknown function.
source: About 20% of PfEMP1 variants belong to group A and are typically longer proteins with a head structure containing DBLα1 and either an EPCR-binding CIDRα1 domain or a CIDRβ/γ/δ domain of unknown function.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the manuscript.

claim: The group A includes two conserved, strain-transcendent subfamilies: the var1 subfamily and the var3 subfamily.
source: Further, the group A includes two conserved, strain-transcendent subfamilies: the var1 subfamily (previously known as var1csa), found in two different variants in the parasite population (3D7- and IT-type) (Otto et al., 2019), and the var3 subfamily, the shortest var genes with only two extracellularly exposed domains (DBLα1.3 and DBLε8).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Otto et al., 2019.

claim: The var1 subfamily is found in two different variants in the parasite population (3D7- and IT-type).
source: Further, the group A includes two conserved, strain-transcendent subfamilies: the var1 subfamily (previously known as var1csa), found in two different variants in the parasite population (3D7- and IT-type) (Otto et al., 2019), and the var3 subfamily, the shortest var genes with only two extracellularly exposed domains (DBLα1.3 and DBLε8).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Otto et al., 2019.

claim: The var3 subfamily are the shortest var genes with only two extracellularly exposed domains (DBLα1.3 and DBLε8).
source: Further, the group A includes two conserved, strain-transcendent subfamilies: the var1 subfamily (previously known as var1csa), found in two different variants in the parasite population (3D7- and IT-type) (Otto et al., 2019), and the var3 subfamily, the shortest var genes with only two extracellularly exposed domains (DBLα1.3 and DBLε8).
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the manuscript.

claim: Groups B and C include most, about 75%, of PfEMP1.
source: Groups B and C include most, about 75%, of PfEMP1 and typically have DBLα0-CIDRα2–6 head structures binding CD36, followed by a DBLδ1-CIDRβ/γ domain combination.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the manuscript.

claim: Groups B and C PfEMP1 typically have DBLα0-CIDRα2–6 head structures binding CD36, followed by a DBLδ1-CIDRβ/γ domain combination.
source: Groups B and C include most, about 75%, of PfEMP1 and typically have DBLα0-CIDRα2–6 head structures binding CD36, followed by a DBLδ1-CIDRβ/γ domain combination.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the manuscript.

claim: A particular subset of B-type proteins, also known as group B/A chimeric genes, possesses a chimeric DBLα0/1 domain and an EPCR-binding CIDRα1 domain.
source: A particular subset of B-type proteins, also known as group B/A chimeric genes, possesses a chimeric DBLα0/1 domain (a.k.a. DBLα2) and an EPCR-binding CIDRα1 domain.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the manuscript.

claim: Specific subsets of DBLβ domains of group A and B PfEMP1 bind ICAM-1.
source: C-terminally to the head structure, most group A and some group B and C PfEMP1 have additional DBL domains, of which specific subsets of DBLβ domains of group A and B PfEMP1 bind ICAM-1 (Lennartz et al., 2017; Janes et al., 2011), and another DBLβ domain, DBLβ12, has been suggested to bind gC1qR (Magallón-Tejada et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lennartz et al., 2017; Janes et al., 2011.

claim: DBLβ12 domain has been suggested to bind gC1qR.
source: C-terminally to the head structure, most group A and some group B and C PfEMP1 have additional DBL domains, of which specific subsets of DBLβ domains of group A and B PfEMP1 bind ICAM-1 (Lennartz et al., 2017; Janes et al., 2011), and another DBLβ domain, DBLβ12, has been suggested to bind gC1qR (Magallón-Tejada et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Magallón-Tejada et al., 2016.

claim: VAR2CSA PfEMP1 (group E, DC2) binds placental CSA and causes pregnancy-associated malaria.
source: The best example of this is the VAR2CSA PfEMP1 (group E, DC2), which binds placental CSA and causes pregnancy-associated malaria (Salanti et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Salanti et al., 2004.

claim: All parasites possess one or two var2csa copies.
source: The VAR2CSA proteins share domain composition, their encoding genes are less diversified than other var groups, and all parasites possess one or two var2csa copies.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the manuscript.

claim: The chimeric group B/A PfEMP1, also known as DC8, includes DBLα2, specific CIDRα1.1/8 subtypes capable to bind EPCR and typically DBLβ12 domains.
source: Another example is the chimeric group B/A PfEMP1, also known as DC8, which includes DBLα2, specific CIDRα1.1/8 subtypes capable to bind EPCR and typically DBLβ12 domains.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the manuscript.

claim: Severe malaria in children is associated with expression of PfEMP1 with EPCR-binding CIDRα1 domains.
source: A consensus from these studies is that severe malaria in children is associated with expression of PfEMP1 with EPCR-binding CIDRα1 domains (Jespersen et al., 2016; Kessler et al., 2017; Storm et al., 2019; Shabani et al., 2017; Mkumbaye et al., 2017; Magallón-Tejada et al., 2016), but elevated expression of dual EPCR and ICAM-1-binding PfEMP1 (Lennartz et al., 2017) and the group A-associated DC5 and DC6 have also been associated with severe disease outcomes (Magallón-Tejada et al., 2016; Avril et al., 2013; Avril et al., 2012; Claessens et al., 2012; Lavstsen et al., 2012; Duffy et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jespersen et al., 2016; Kessler et al., 2017; Storm et al., 2019; Shabani et al., 2017; Mkumbaye et al., 2017; Magallón-Tejada et al., 2016.

claim: Elevated expression of dual EPCR and ICAM-1-binding PfEMP1 has been associated with severe disease outcomes.
source: A consensus from these studies is that severe malaria in children is associated with expression of PfEMP1 with EPCR-binding CIDRα1 domains (Jespersen et al., 2016; Kessler et al., 2017; Storm et al., 2019; Shabani et al., 2017; Mkumbaye et al., 2017; Magallón-Tejada et al., 2016), but elevated expression of dual EPCR and ICAM-1-binding PfEMP1 (Lennartz et al., 2017) and the group A-associated DC5 and DC6 have also been associated with severe disease outcomes (Magallón-Tejada et al., 2016; Avril et al., 2013; Avril et al., 2012; Claessens et al., 2012; Lavstsen et al., 2012; Duffy et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lennartz et al., 2017.

claim: The group A-associated DC5 and DC6 have been associated with severe disease outcomes.
source: A consensus from these studies is that severe malaria in children is associated with expression of PfEMP1 with EPCR-binding CIDRα1 domains (Jespersen et al., 2016; Kessler et al., 2017; Storm et al., 2019; Shabani et al., 2017; Mkumbaye et al., 2017; Magallón-Tejada et al., 2016), but elevated expression of dual EPCR and ICAM-1-binding PfEMP1 (Lennartz et al., 2017) and the group A-associated DC5 and DC6 have also been associated with severe disease outcomes (Magallón-Tejada et al., 2016; Avril et al., 2013; Avril et al., 2012; Claessens et al., 2012; Lavstsen et al., 2012; Duffy et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Magallón-Tejada et al., 2016; Avril et al., 2013; Avril et al., 2012; Claessens et al., 2012; Lavstsen et al., 2012; Duffy et al., 2019.

claim: Two gene expression studies from regions of unstable transmission in India showed elevated expression of EPCR-binding variants (DC8, DC13) and DC6.
source: Two gene expression studies from regions of unstable transmission in India showed elevated expression of EPCR-binding variants (DC8, DC13) and DC6 (Bernabeu et al., 2016; Subudhi et al., 2015), and also of transcripts encoding B- and C-type PfEMP1 in severe cases (Subudhi et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bernabeu et al., 2016; Subudhi et al., 2015.

claim: Transcripts encoding B- and C-type PfEMP1 were elevated in severe cases in India.
source: Two gene expression studies from regions of unstable transmission in India showed elevated expression of EPCR-binding variants (DC8, DC13) and DC6 (Bernabeu et al., 2016; Subudhi et al., 2015), and also of transcripts encoding B- and C-type PfEMP1 in severe cases (Subudhi et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Subudhi et al., 2015.

claim: The study analyzed RNA-seq profiles of parasites isolated from 32 P. falciparum-infected adult travellers returning to Germany.
source: Here, we analyzed RNA-seq profiles of parasites isolated from 32 P. falciparum-infected adult travellers returning to Germany.

claim: Patients were categorized into severe (n = 8) or non-severe (n = 24) cases.
source: Patients were categorized into either malaria naive (n = 15) or pre-exposed (n = 17), and into severe (n = 8) or non-severe (n = 24) cases.
evidence: The claim describes the study design and patient categorization.

claim: Severe malaria was associated with PfEMP1 containing the EPCR-binding CIDRα1 domain.
source: Both approaches showed in concordance that severe malaria was associated with PfEMP1 containing the endothelial protein C receptor (EPCR)-binding CIDRα1 domain, whereas CD36-binding PfEMP1 was linked to non-severe malaria outcomes.

claim: CD36-binding PfEMP1 was linked to non-severe malaria outcomes.
source: Both approaches showed in concordance that severe malaria was associated with PfEMP1 containing the endothelial protein C receptor (EPCR)-binding CIDRα1 domain, whereas CD36-binding PfEMP1 was linked to non-severe malaria outcomes.

claim: Immune responses to AMA1 and MSP1 are known to be long-lasting.
source: Immune responses to AMA1 and MSP1 are known to be long-lasting, and seroconversion to AMA1 is assumed to occur only after a single or very few infections (Drakeley et al., 2005).

claim: Seroconversion to AMA1 is assumed to occur only after a single or very few infections.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Drakeley et al., 2005.

claim: Principal component analysis (PCA) of the Luminex data resulted in separation of the patients into two discrete groups corresponding to first-time infected adults ('naive cluster') and malaria pre-exposed individuals ('pre-exposed cluster').
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) of the Luminex data resulted in separation of the patients into two discrete groups corresponding to first-time infected adults ('naive cluster') and malaria pre-exposed individuals ('pre-exposed cluster') (Figure 1A).

claim: The 13 patients with an unknown malaria exposure status could be grouped into either the naive or the pre-exposed group defined by the PCA of antigen reactivity.
source: The 13 patients with an unknown malaria exposure status could be grouped into either the naive or the pre-exposed group defined by the PCA of antigen reactivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from PCA analysis.

claim: Patient #21 was the only outlier in the clustering.
source: The only outlier in the clustering was a 19-year-old patient (#21) from Sudan, who reported several malaria episodes during childhood, but clustered with the malaria-naive patients.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from PCA analysis.

claim: Patient #21 is a 19-year-old from Sudan who reported several malaria episodes during childhood, but clustered with the malaria-naive patients.
source: The only outlier in the clustering was a 19-year-old patient (#21) from Sudan, who reported several malaria episodes during childhood, but clustered with the malaria-naive patients.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from PCA analysis and patient history.

claim: Pre-exposed patients showed higher antibody levels against tested P. falciparum antigens.
source: With exception of patient #21, unsupervised clustering of the PCA-reduced data clearly discriminates between first-time infected (naive) and pre-exposed patients with higher antibody levels against tested P. falciparum antigens and also assigns plasma samples from patients with an unknown immune status into naive and pre-exposed clusters (A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Serological assays revealed significant differences between patient groups.
source: Serological assays revealed significant differences between patient groups (Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of serological data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The mADRB, ELISA, and Luminex assays are most relevant in the prediction of patient clusters.
source: The variable importance plot of the random forest model shows the decrease in prediction accuracy if values of a variable are permuted randomly. The decrease in accuracy was determined for each serological assay, indicating that the mADRB, ELISA, and Luminex assays are most relevant in the prediction of patient clusters (F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from random forest analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Pre-exposed individuals showed significantly elevated IgG antibody responses against a broad range of parasite antigens.
source: As expected, pre-exposed individuals showed significantly elevated IgG antibody responses against a broad range of parasite antigens, especially typical parasite blood stage markers, including MSP1, MSP2, MSP4, MSP10, EBA175, REX1, and AMA1 (Figure 1D, upper panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from protein microarray analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Markers for a recent infection, MSP1, MSP4, GLURP, and ETRAMP5, were significantly elevated in the pre-exposed individuals in comparison to the defined first-time infected group.
source: Markers for a recent infection, MSP1, MSP4, GLURP, and ETRAMP5 (van den Hoogen et al., 2018), were significantly elevated in the pre-exposed individuals in comparison to the defined first-time infected group.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from protein microarray analysis and a citation to van den Hoogen et al., 2018.

claim: Antibodies against pre-erythrocytic antigens, such as CSP, STARP, and LSA3, were highly elevated in pre-exposed individuals.
source: In addition, further members of the ETRAMP family, including ETRAMP10, ETRAMP14, ETRAMP10.2, and ETRAMP4, and also antibodies against pre-erythrocytic antigens, such as CSP, STARP, and LSA3, were highly elevated.

claim: Eight patients from the malaria-naive group were considered as having severe malaria based on the predefined criteria.

claim: Elevated antibody levels were found in the severe subgroup when comparing the IgG antibody response of severe and non-severe cases within the previously malaria-naive group.
source: Comparing the IgG antibody response of severe and non-severe cases within the previously malaria-naive group, elevated antibody levels were found in the severe subgroup.

claim: The highest fold change in antibody levels in severe cases was observed for antibodies directed against intracellular proteins, such as DnaJ protein, GTPase-activating protein, or heat shock protein 70.
source: The highest fold change was observed for antibodies directed against intracellular proteins, such as DnaJ protein, GTPase-activating protein, or heat shock protein 70 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: IgM antibodies against ETRAMP5 were detectable in the severely infected individuals, suggesting they were infected for a prolonged period of time compared to the mild malaria population.
source: Interestingly, IgM antibodies against ETRAMP5 were detectable in the severely infected individuals, suggesting they were infected for a prolonged period of time compared to the mild malaria population (Helb et al., 2015; van den Hoogen et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from protein microarray analysis and citations to Helb et al., 2015; van den Hoogen et al., 2018.

claim: Transcriptome libraries were sequenced for all 32 patient samples.

source: The number of trimmed reads ranged between 29,142,684 and 82,000,248 (median: 41,383,289) within the individual libraries derived from patients.

source: The proportion of total reads specific for P. falciparum was 87.7% (median; IQR 76.7–91.3) for the 30 samples included in the de novo assembly (Supplementary file 3).

claim: Parasites from first-time infected and pre-exposed patients revealed no obvious difference in the proportion of the different parasite stages or in median age.

evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Table 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A small, statistically not significant bias (p=0.17) towards younger parasites in the severe cases was observed with a median age of 8.2 hours post infection (hpi) (IQR 8.0–9.8) in comparison to 9.8 hpi in the non-severe cases (IQR 8.2–11.4).
source: However, a small, statistically not significant bias (p=0.17) towards younger parasites in the severe cases was observed with a median age of 8.2 hours post infection (hpi) (IQR 8.0–9.8) in comparison to 9.8 hpi in the non-severe cases (IQR 8.2–11.4) (Table 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Table 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: None of the samples revealed high proportions of late trophozoites (all <3%), schizonts (0%), or gametocytes (all <6%).
source: None of the samples revealed high proportions of late trophozoites (all <3%), schizonts (0%), or gametocytes (all <6%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).

claim: Global gene expression analysis identified 420 genes to be higher and 236 to be lower expressed (p≤0.05) in first-time infected patients, together corresponding to 11.3% of all P. falciparum genes.

evidence: The claim is supported by data from differential gene expression analysis.

claim: 362 genes were significantly higher and 219 genes lower expressed in severe cases.
source: Similarly, 362 genes were significantly higher and 219 genes lower expressed in severe cases (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from differential gene expression analysis.

claim: The KEGG pathway 03410 'base excision repair' was expressed at significantly higher levels in first-time infected patient samples.
source: A gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of the differentially expressed genes using Gene Ontology (GO) terms and KEGG pathway annotations showed that the KEGG pathway 03410 'base excision repair' facilitating the maintenance of genome integrity by repairing small base lesions in the DNA was expressed at significantly higher levels in first-time infected patient samples (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from GSEA shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Six out of 15 P. falciparum genes included in the KEGG pathway 03410 'base excision repair' were found to be statistically significantly enriched upon first-time infection.
source: In total, six out of 15 P. falciparum genes included in this KEGG pathway were found to be statistically significantly enriched upon first-time infection, including the putative endonuclease III (PF3D7_0614800) from the short-patch pathway and the putative A-/G-specific adenine glycosylase (PF3D7_1129500), the putative apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease Apn1 (PF3D7_1332600), the proliferating cell nuclear antigens 1 (PF3D7_1361900), and the catalytic (PF3D7_1017000) and small (PF3D7_0308000) subunits from the DNA polymerase delta from the long-patch pathway (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A significantly lower expression level for genes associated with several GO terms involved in antigenic variation and host cell remodeling was found in first-time infected patients.
source: Additionally, a significantly lower expression level for genes associated with several GO terms involved in antigenic variation and host cell remodeling was found in first-time infected patients (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 4) and severe cases (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from GSEA shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In total, 6441 var contigs with over 500 bp lengths were generated with an N50 of 2302 bp and a maximum length of 10,412 bp.
source: In total, 6441 contigs with over 500 bp lengths were generated with an N50 of 2302 bp and a maximum length of 10,412 bp (Source data 1.).
evidence: The claim describes the results of var gene assembly.

claim: A median of 200 contigs (IQR: 137–279) with lengths >500 bp was assembled per sample.
source: A median of 200 contigs (IQR: 137–279) with lengths >500 bp was assembled per sample.
evidence: The claim describes the results of var gene assembly.

claim: One or more DBL or CIDR domains could be annotated to 5488 of the contigs.
source: One or more DBL or CIDR domains could be annotated to 5488 of the contigs, whereas the remaining contigs could only be annotated by these smaller domain building blocks, the so-called homology blocks as defined by Rask et al., 2010; Supplementary file 6, 7.
evidence: The claim describes the results of var gene annotation.

claim: The var1-IT variant was expressed at higher levels in parasites from first-time infected patients.
source: Notably, the var1-IT variant was expressed at higher levels in parasites from first-time infected patients, whereas the var1-3D7 variant was expressed at higher levels in parasites from pre-exposed and non-severe patients (Figure 4A,B, Figure 5A,B, Supplementary file 9, 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 4A,B and 5A,B.

claim: The var1-3D7 variant was expressed at higher levels in parasites from pre-exposed and non-severe patients.
source: Notably, the var1-IT variant was expressed at higher levels in parasites from first-time infected patients, whereas the var1-3D7 variant was expressed at higher levels in parasites from pre-exposed and non-severe patients (Figure 4A,B, Figure 5A,B, Supplementary file 9, 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 4A,B and 5A,B.

claim: Different EPCR-binding CIDRα1 domain variants and other domains found in DC with CIDRα1 domains were expressed at significantly higher levels in first-time infected patients.
source: This showed that different EPCR-binding CIDRα1 domain variants and other domains found in DC with CIDRα1 domains were expressed at significantly higher levels in first-time infected patients (Figure 4C–E, Supplementary file 9).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C–E.

claim: Domains from DC8 (DBLα2, CIDRα1.1, DBLβ12) and DC13 (DBLα1.7, CIDRα1.4) were increased upon infection of malaria-naive individuals.
source: Specifically, besides domains from DC8 (DBLα2, CIDRα1.1, DBLβ12) and DC13 (DBLα1.7, CIDRα1.4), the CIDRα1.7 and DBLα1.2 (DC15) domains were increased upon infection of malaria-naive individuals.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from differential domain expression analysis.

claim: The CIDRα1.7 and DBLα1.2 (DC15) domains were increased upon infection of malaria-naive individuals.
source: Specifically, besides domains from DC8 (DBLα2, CIDRα1.1, DBLβ12) and DC13 (DBLα1.7, CIDRα1.4), the CIDRα1.7 and DBLα1.2 (DC15) domains were increased upon infection of malaria-naive individuals.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from differential domain expression analysis.

claim: The DBLα1.2 domain was, in all of the 32 gene assemblies, flanked by an EPCR-binding CIDRα1 domain, and 56% of these were a CIDRα1.5 domain.
source: The DBLα1.2 domain was, in all of the 32 gene assemblies, flanked by an EPCR-binding CIDRα1 domain, and 56% of these were a CIDRα1.5 domain (Supplementary file 6, 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from var gene assembly analysis.

claim: Parasites from first-time infected patients showed a significantly higher level of transcripts encoding the CIDRδ1 domain of DC16 (DBLα1.5/6-CIDRδ1/2) and the DBLβ6 domain.
source: In addition, parasites from first-time infected patients showed a significantly higher level of transcripts encoding the CIDRδ1 domain of DC16 (DBLα1.5/6-CIDRδ1/2) and the DBLβ6 domain (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D–E.

claim: Domains found expressed at lower levels in malaria-naive individuals included group B and C N-terminal head structure domains NTSB and DBLα0.13/22/23, and CD36-binding CIDR domains (CIDRα2.8/9,6) as well as the C-terminal CIDRγ11 domain and domains of the var1-3D7 variant (DBLα1.4, DBLγ15, DBLε5).
source: Domains found expressed at lower levels in malaria-naive individuals included group B and C N-terminal head structure domains NTSB and DBLα0.13/22/23, and CD36-binding CIDR domains (CIDRα2.8/9,6) as well as the C-terminal CIDRγ11 domain and domains of the var1-3D7 variant (DBLα1.4, DBLγ15, DBLε5) (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C–E.

claim: Domains of DC8 (DBLα2, CIDRα1.1, DBLβ12), DC15 (DBLα1.2), and DC16 (DBLα1.6) and the A-type-linked DBLβ6 were found associated with severe disease.
source: When comparing severe to the non-severe cases, domains of DC8 (DBLα2, CIDRα1.1, DBLβ12), DC15 (DBLα1.2), and DC16 (DBLα1.6) and the A-type-linked DBLβ6 were found associated with severe disease.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from differential domain expression analysis.

claim: Domain types expressed at significantly higher levels in non-severe cases included N-terminal head structure domains, DBLα0.23, CIDRα2.4/9 from group B and C PfEMP1, DC16 (DBLα1.5), and the CIDRα1.3 domain from the var1-3D7 allele.
source: Domain types expressed at significantly higher levels in non-severe cases included N-terminal head structure domains, DBLα0.23, CIDRα2.4/9 from group B and C PfEMP1, DC16 (DBLα1.5), and the CIDRα1.3 domain from the var1-3D7 allele (Figure 5C–E, Supplementary file 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C–E.

claim: Domains associated with EPCR-binding as well as the CIDRγ3 domain were expressed at higher levels in naive and more severe cases.
source: This showed significant differences for domains associated with EPCR- or CD36-binding PfEMP1. As expected, domains associated with EPCR-binding as well as the CIDRγ3 domain were expressed at higher levels in naive and more severe cases, whereas domains associated with the CD36-binding phenotype were higher expressed in pre-exposed and non-severe patients.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from analysis of N-terminal head structure domains grouped by binding phenotype.

claim: Domains associated with the CD36-binding phenotype were higher expressed in pre-exposed and non-severe patients.
source: This showed significant differences for domains associated with EPCR- or CD36-binding PfEMP1. As expected, domains associated with EPCR-binding as well as the CIDRγ3 domain were expressed at higher levels in naive and more severe cases, whereas domains associated with the CD36-binding phenotype were higher expressed in pre-exposed and non-severe patients.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from analysis of N-terminal head structure domains grouped by binding phenotype.

claim: Transcripts encoding block numbers 255, 584, and 614, all typically located within DBLβ domains of DC8- and CIDRα1-containing type A PfEMP1, were found associated with a naive immune status.
source: Transcripts encoding block numbers 255, 584, and 614, all typically located within DBLβ domains of DC8- and CIDRα1-containing type A PfEMP1 (Figure 4G,H, Supplementary file 9), number 557, located in the interdomain region between DBLβ and DBLγ domains (no PfEMP1 type association), and block number 155, found in NTSA, were found associated with a naive immune status.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4G,H.

claim: Transcripts encoding block number 88 from DBLα0 domains and 269 from ATSB were found at lower levels in malaria-naive patients, indicating that B- and C-type genes are more frequently expressed in pre-exposed individuals.
source: Conversely, transcripts encoding block number 88 from DBLα0 domains and 269 from ATSB were found at lower levels in malaria-naive patients, indicating that B- and C-type genes are more frequently expressed in pre-exposed individuals (Figure 4G,H, Supplementary file 9).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4G,H and includes an inference.

claim: No homology blocks were associated with severe cases.
source: No homology blocks were associated with severe cases, but two blocks, 591 and 559, found in group B PfEMP1, were found to be lower expressed in severe malaria cases (Figure 5G,H, Supplementary file 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5G,H.

claim: Two blocks, 591 and 559, found in group B PfEMP1, were found to be lower expressed in severe malaria cases.
source: No homology blocks were associated with severe cases, but two blocks, 591 and 559, found in group B PfEMP1, were found to be lower expressed in severe malaria cases (Figure 5G,H, Supplementary file 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5G,H.

claim: Between 851 and 3368 reads with a median of 1666 over all samples were analyzed from DBLα-tag sequencing.
source: Between 851 and 3368 reads with a median of 1666 over all samples were analyzed.
evidence: The claim describes the results of DBLα-tag sequencing.

claim: The relative expression levels were similar for sequences found in both the RNA-seq and the DBLα-tag approach with a mean log2(DBLα-PCR/RNA-seq) ratio of 0.4 (CI of 95%: −2.5–3.3).
source: Overall, the relative expression levels were similar for sequences found in both the RNA-seq and the DBLα-tag approach with a mean log2(DBLα-PCR/RNA-seq) ratio of 0.4 (CI of 95%: −2.5–3.3) determined by Bland-Altman plotting (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Around 82.6% (median) of all unique DBLα-tag sequences detected with >10 reads (92.9% of all DBLα-tag sequences) were found in the RNA-seq approach.
source: Around 82.6% (median) of all unique DBLα-tag sequences detected with >10 reads (92.9% of all DBLα-tag sequences) were found in the RNA-seq approach, and 81.8% of the upper 75th percentile of RNA-seq contigs (spanning across the DBLα-tag region) were found by the DBLα-tag approach.
evidence: The claim describes the concordance between RNA-seq and DBLα-tag approaches.

claim: 81.8% of the upper 75th percentile of RNA-seq contigs (spanning across the DBLα-tag region) were found by the DBLα-tag approach.
source: Around 82.6% (median) of all unique DBLα-tag sequences detected with >10 reads (92.9% of all DBLα-tag sequences) were found in the RNA-seq approach, and 81.8% of the upper 75th percentile of RNA-seq contigs (spanning across the DBLα-tag region) were found by the DBLα-tag approach.
evidence: The claim describes the concordance between RNA-seq and DBLα-tag approaches.

claim: A partial domain annotation was made for ~85% of the DBLα-tag sequences.
source: A partial domain annotation was made for ~85% of the DBLα-tag sequences (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 11).
evidence: The claim describes the results of domain prediction from DBLα-tag sequences.

claim: DBLα1 and DBLα2 sequences were enriched in first-time infected and severe malaria patients.
source: In line with the RNA-seq data, this analysis showed that DBLα1 and DBLα2 sequences were enriched in first-time infected and severe malaria patients.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from DBLα-tag analysis.

claim: A significant higher proportion of DBLα0 sequences was found in pre-exposed individuals and mild cases.
source: Conversely, a significant higher proportion of DBLα0 sequences was found in pre-exposed individuals and mild cases (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: A significantly higher proportion of NTSA was found in severe cases.
source: Prediction of the NTS and CIDR domains flanking the DBLα domain showed a significantly higher proportion of NTSA in severe cases as well as EPCR-binding CIDRα1 domains in first-time infected and severe cases.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from DBLα-tag domain prediction analysis.

claim: EPCR-binding CIDRα1 domains were found at higher proportions in first-time infected and severe cases.
source: Prediction of the NTS and CIDR domains flanking the DBLα domain showed a significantly higher proportion of NTSA in severe cases as well as EPCR-binding CIDRα1 domains in first-time infected and severe cases.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from DBLα-tag domain prediction analysis.

claim: Expression of var genes encoding NTSB and CIDRα2–6 domains was significantly associated within pre-exposed and non-severe cases.
source: Expression of var genes encoding NTSB and CIDRα2–6 domains was significantly associated within pre-exposed and non-severe cases (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Var transcripts with DBLβ, γ, and ζ or CIDRγ domains were more frequently expressed in first-time infected and severe malaria patients.
source: Subsequent analysis of var expression in relation to other domains showed that var transcripts with DBLβ, γ, and ζ or CIDRγ domains were more frequently expressed in first-time infected and severe malaria patients whereas those encoding DBLδ and CIDRβ were less frequent (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Var transcripts encoding DBLδ and CIDRβ were less frequent in first-time infected and severe malaria patients.
source: Subsequent analysis of var expression in relation to other domains showed that var transcripts with DBLβ, γ, and ζ or CIDRγ domains were more frequently expressed in first-time infected and severe malaria patients whereas those encoding DBLδ and CIDRβ were less frequent (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: CIDRα1.1/5, DBLβ12, DBLγ2/12, DBLα2, DBLα1.2/2, and DBLδ5 were found associated with severe malaria.
source: Assessing expression in relation to the domain subtype, CIDRα1.1/5, DBLβ12, DBLγ2/12, DBLα2, DBLα1.2/2, and DBLδ5 (together with DBLγ12 components of the DC5) were found associated with severe malaria, while CIDRα3.1/4, DBLα0.12/16, and DBLδ1 were associated with non-severe cases (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: CIDRα3.1/4, DBLα0.12/16, and DBLδ1 were associated with non-severe cases.
source: Assessing expression in relation to the domain subtype, CIDRα1.1/5, DBLβ12, DBLγ2/12, DBLα2, DBLα1.2/2, and DBLδ5 (together with DBLγ12 components of the DC5) were found associated with severe malaria, while CIDRα3.1/4, DBLα0.12/16, and DBLδ1 were associated with non-severe cases (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Plasma samples from malaria-naive as well as severe cases showed lower mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) values for all antigens tested in comparison to samples from pre-exposed or non-severe cases.
source: In general, plasma samples from malaria-naive as well as severe cases showed lower mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) values for all antigens tested in comparison to samples from pre-exposed or non-severe cases with significant differences for CIDRα2–6, CIDRδ1, and CIDRγ3, but not for EPCR-binding CIDRα1 domains (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: Significant differences in antibody recognition were observed for CIDRα2–6, CIDRδ1, and CIDRγ3, but not for EPCR-binding CIDRα1 domains.
source: In general, plasma samples from malaria-naive as well as severe cases showed lower mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) values for all antigens tested in comparison to samples from pre-exposed or non-severe cases with significant differences for CIDRα2–6, CIDRδ1, and CIDRγ3, but not for EPCR-binding CIDRα1 domains (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: Almost half of the tested antigens were recognized by pre-exposed (median: 47.2%) and non-severe patients (median: 44.4%).
source: In this analysis, almost half of the tested antigens were recognized by pre-exposed (median: 47.2%) and non-severe patients (median: 44.4%), but only 1/4 of the antigens were recognized by first-time infected patients (median: 25.0%) and 1/20 by severely ill patients (median: 5.6%).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from antibody breadth analysis.

claim: Only 1/4 of the antigens were recognized by first-time infected patients (median: 25.0%).
source: In this analysis, almost half of the tested antigens were recognized by pre-exposed (median: 47.2%) and non-severe patients (median: 44.4%), but only 1/4 of the antigens were recognized by first-time infected patients (median: 25.0%) and 1/20 by severely ill patients (median: 5.6%).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from antibody breadth analysis.

claim: Only 1/20 of the antigens were recognized by severely ill patients (median: 5.6%).
source: In this analysis, almost half of the tested antigens were recognized by pre-exposed (median: 47.2%) and non-severe patients (median: 44.4%), but only 1/4 of the antigens were recognized by first-time infected patients (median: 25.0%) and 1/20 by severely ill patients (median: 5.6%).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from antibody breadth analysis.

claim: PfEMP1 antigens recognized by over 60% of the pre-exposed and/or non-severe patient sera were four CIDRα1 domains capable of EPCR-binding (CIDRα1.5, CIDRα1.6, CIDRα1.7, and the DC8 domain CIDRα1.8), two CD36-binding CIDRα domains (CIDRα2.10, CIDRα3.1), and two CIDR domains with unknown binding phenotypes (CIDRδ1 and CIDRγ3).
source: PfEMP1 antigens recognized by over 60% of the pre-exposed and/or non-severe patient sera were (i) four CIDRα1 domains capable of EPCR-binding (CIDRα1.5, CIDRα1.6, CIDRα1.7, and the DC8 domain CIDRα1.8), (ii) two CD36-binding CIDRα domains (CIDRα2.10, CIDRα3.1), and (iii) two CIDR domains with unknown binding phenotypes (CIDRδ1 and CIDRγ3) (Figure 7C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Higher levels of antibodies against severe malaria-associated EPCR-binding variants are present in pre-exposed and non-severe cases, which might have selected against parasites expressing CIDRα1 domains during the current infection.
source: Taken together, this analysis indicates that higher levels of antibodies against severe malaria-associated EPCR-binding variants are present in pre-exposed and non-severe cases, which might have selected against parasites expressing CIDRα1 domains during the current infection.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the antibody data with a speculative component.

claim: Our data confirmed previously reported associations between transcripts encoding type A and B EPCR-binding PfEMP1 and infections in naive hosts and disease severity.
source: Despite the relatively low number of patient samples recruited in 5 years, our data confirmed previously reported associations between transcripts encoding type A and B EPCR-binding PfEMP1 and infections in naive hosts and disease severity (Duffy et al., 2019; Tonkin-Hill et al., 2018; Kessler et al., 2017; Bernabeu et al., 2016; Jespersen et al., 2016; Lavstsen et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study and citations to previous studies.

claim: Our results suggest that parasite interaction with EPCR is linked to severe disease in children as well as in adults.
source: Our results further suggest that parasite interaction with EPCR is linked to severe disease in children as well as in adults.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the study data.

claim: Since CIDRα1-containing PfEMP1 possess multiple binding traits, co-interaction with other receptors may further increase the risk for severe malaria.
source: However, since CIDRα1-containing PfEMP1 possess multiple binding traits (Lennartz et al., 2017; Magallón-Tejada et al., 2016), co-interaction with other receptors may further increase the risk for severe malaria.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to Lennartz et al., 2017; Magallón-Tejada et al., 2016.

claim: Paediatric cerebral malaria infections are dominated by the expansion of parasites expressing EPCR-binding domains accompanied by parasites expressing other group A PfEMP1, possibly acting as rosetting variants.
source: However, together with previous observations, our data suggest that paediatric cerebral malaria infections are dominated by the expansion of parasites expressing EPCR-binding domains accompanied by parasites expressing other group A PfEMP1, possibly acting as rosetting variants.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the study data combined with previous observations.

claim: IgG against EPCR-binding CIDR domains were acquired before IgG to other CIDR domains.
source: This was consistent with the more frequent recognition of CIDRα1 domains than CIDRα2–6 domains in pre-exposed patients, indicating that IgG against EPCR-binding CIDR domains were acquired before IgG to other CIDR domains, as has been observed for malaria endemic populations (Obeng-Adjei et al., 2020; Cham et al., 2009; Cham et al., 2010; Turner et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the antibody data supported by citations to Obeng-Adjei et al., 2020; Cham et al., 2009; Cham et al., 2010; Turner et al., 2015.

claim: A high expression of A- and B-type var genes and an association of DC4, -8, and -13 with disease severity has been reported for malaria cases imported to France.
source: A high expression of A- and B-type var genes and an association of DC4, -8, and -13 with disease severity has been reported for malaria cases imported to France (Argy et al., 2017), and parasites from severe Indian adults show an elevated expression of DC6, -8 (Bernabeu et al., 2016), and DC13 (Subudhi et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Argy et al., 2017.

claim: Parasites from severe Indian adults show an elevated expression of DC6, -8, and DC13.
source: A high expression of A- and B-type var genes and an association of DC4, -8, and -13 with disease severity has been reported for malaria cases imported to France (Argy et al., 2017), and parasites from severe Indian adults show an elevated expression of DC6, -8 (Bernabeu et al., 2016), and DC13 (Subudhi et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bernabeu et al., 2016 and Subudhi et al., 2015.

claim: In the severe cases from Indonesia, mainly the DCs 4, 8, and 11 were found on an elevated level.
source: In the severe cases from Indonesia, mainly the DCs 4, 8, and 11 were found on an elevated level (Tonkin-Hill et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tonkin-Hill et al., 2018.

claim: All studies are in agreement with the expression data from our cohort of adult travellers.
source: All studies are in agreement with the expression data from our cohort of adult travellers, although we here in addition found a higher expression of DC15 (EPCR binding) and DC16 (putative rosetting variants) var genes in malaria-naive patients.
evidence: The claim is a comparison of the study data with previous studies.

claim: We found a higher expression of DC15 (EPCR binding) and DC16 (putative rosetting variants) var genes in malaria-naive patients.
source: All studies are in agreement with the expression data from our cohort of adult travellers, although we here in addition found a higher expression of DC15 (EPCR binding) and DC16 (putative rosetting variants) var genes in malaria-naive patients.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: There is cumulative evidence that CIDRα1-containing transcripts are dominating the infection in children with severe malaria, severe anemia, and cerebral malaria.
source: Measurements of the total abundances of the different var groups are challenging (e.g., due differences in the coverage or sensitivity of qPCR or DBLα-tag primer pairs targeting the different var groups), but there is cumulative evidence that CIDRα1-containing transcripts are dominating the infection in children with severe malaria, severe anemia, and cerebral malaria, and transcripts with CIDRα2–6 domains are most abundantly expressed during uncomplicated malaria (Jespersen et al., 2016; Duffy et al., 2019; Warimwe et al., 2009; Warimwe et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jespersen et al., 2016; Duffy et al., 2019; Warimwe et al., 2009; Warimwe et al., 2012.

claim: Transcripts with CIDRα2–6 domains are most abundantly expressed during uncomplicated malaria.
source: Measurements of the total abundances of the different var groups are challenging (e.g., due differences in the coverage or sensitivity of qPCR or DBLα-tag primer pairs targeting the different var groups), but there is cumulative evidence that CIDRα1-containing transcripts are dominating the infection in children with severe malaria, severe anemia, and cerebral malaria, and transcripts with CIDRα2–6 domains are most abundantly expressed during uncomplicated malaria (Jespersen et al., 2016; Duffy et al., 2019; Warimwe et al., 2009; Warimwe et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jespersen et al., 2016; Duffy et al., 2019; Warimwe et al., 2009; Warimwe et al., 2012.

claim: In most of our adult patients, CD36-binding var transcripts appear to dominate the expression pattern.
source: Although the median expression of CIDRα2–6 is lower in first-time infected and severe cases compared to pre-exposed and non-severe cases, in most of our adult patients, CD36-binding var transcripts appear to dominate the expression pattern.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the study data.

claim: All three other adult studies indicate a substantial expression of B- and C-type variants associated with the binding of CD36.
source: This is in concordance with all three other adult studies also indicating a substantial expression of B- and C-type variants associated with the binding of CD36 (Argy et al., 2017; Bernabeu et al., 2016; Subudhi et al., 2015), and (Subudhi et al., 2015) even showed an association with complicated adult malaria.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Argy et al., 2017; Bernabeu et al., 2016; Subudhi et al., 2015.

claim: Subudhi et al., 2015 showed an association of B- and C-type variants with complicated adult malaria.
source: This is in concordance with all three other adult studies also indicating a substantial expression of B- and C-type variants associated with the binding of CD36 (Argy et al., 2017; Bernabeu et al., 2016; Subudhi et al., 2015), and (Subudhi et al., 2015) even showed an association with complicated adult malaria.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Subudhi et al., 2015.

claim: Parasite binding to CD36 may be specifically enhanced in adult severe malaria cases compared to children.
source: Maybe parasite binding to CD36 is specifically enhanced in adult severe malaria cases compared to children, which is interesting due to their different disease symptomatology (Dondorp et al., 2008; Schwartz et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to Dondorp et al., 2008; Schwartz et al., 2001.

claim: Our adult cohort differs not only in age but also in terms of disease severity from paediatric cohorts, and less sick patients may simply have a less dominant expression of EPCR-binding variants.
source: Alternatively, our adult cohort differs not only in age but also in terms of disease severity from paediatric cohorts, and less sick patients may simply have a less dominant expression of EPCR-binding variants.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the study data.

claim: For the parasite's survival and transmission, it may be highly beneficial to express more of the less virulent PfEMP1 variants that are able to bind CD36.
source: However, for the parasite's survival and transmission, it may be highly beneficial to express more of the less virulent PfEMP1 variants that are able to bind CD36.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation.

claim: CD36 interaction may not, or is less likely to, result in obstruction of blood flow, inflammation, and organ failure at least of the brain, where CD36 is nearly absent.
source: This interaction may not, or is less likely to, result in obstruction of blood flow, inflammation, and organ failure at least of the brain, where CD36 is nearly absent (Turner et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation to Turner et al., 1994.

claim: This study is the first description of expression differences between the two var1 variants, 3D7 and IT.
source: To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first description of expression differences between the two var1 variants, 3D7 and IT.
evidence: The claim is stated as a novel finding in the manuscript.

claim: The var1 subfamily is ubiquitously transcribed.
source: In general, the var1 subfamily is ubiquitously transcribed (Winter et al., 2003; Duffy et al., 2006), atypically late in the cell cycle after transcription of var genes encoding the adhesion phenotype (Kyes et al., 2003; Duffy et al., 2002; Dahlbäck et al., 2007) and is annotated as a pseudogene in 3D7 due to a premature stop codon.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Winter et al., 2003; Duffy et al., 2006.

claim: CD36-binding variants are still overrepresented in all groups of adult malaria patients.
